intro.text: Everything you've practiced so far comes together in this chapter: we kick off the course's capstone project, Ohana Link — a bookmark service where users save the pages they visit often and organize them into folders. Working on top of Next.js, you'll direct Claude to build the base UI, apply a professional design theme with Claude's Skills feature, and then deliver the app's first real features: full folder management and link management, including the project's first home-made API. Your role is the manager's role: write a clear spec, then judge what comes back. Along the way you'll practice the rhythm professional teams use: request one feature, verify it in the browser, commit, push, repeat.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: This chapter assumes you have the Next.js project from the previous chapters — the `ohana-link` project folder created with create-next-app, with Claude Code set up and the repository connected to GitHub. If you skipped ahead, go back and complete that setup first.

lessons.title: Project Introduction
lessons.objective: Get to know Ohana Link — the bookmark service you'll have Claude build for the rest of the course — its key features, and how the lessons will teach new concepts exactly when the project needs them. Knowing the target this well is what lets you judge every delivery against it.

blocks.text: Starting in this chapter, we build the course's final project — Ohana Link — together, with Claude doing the coding and you directing and reviewing. Ohana Link is a bookmark service: a place to store the pages you keep coming back to and manage them with folders. We'll build it on top of Next.js, step by step, into something close to a real production service.

Before requesting any code, spend a few minutes playing with the finished demo so you know exactly what you're asking for — a manager who knows the target can spot the gaps in a delivery. Click the folders in the sidebar to filter links, and try adding your own with the + New Folder and + New Link buttons. (The instructor demo at ohana-link.vercel.app is the original Korean-language version — the layout and features are exactly what your project will have.)

steps.title: What kind of project is it?

blocks.text: A bookmark service where users save links they like and file them into folders (Design / Dev / AI, and so on).
It looks like a small project, but it's deliberately designed to touch a wide range of the core concepts you need for real web development.
Link CRUD — create, read, update, and delete links.
Folder management — create folders and filter links by folder.
Database integration — store data permanently so you see the same links no matter which device you sign in from.
CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations almost every data-driven app performs. When developers say “link CRUD,” they mean the full life cycle of a link record.
Rather than studying theory first, we'll learn each core concept at the moment the project needs it:
When we reach the point where data must be saved, we'll dig into databases.
At the end of the course, you'll step back from the project to learn how authentication and authorization work — the concepts behind user accounts and data protection.
The project is designed so these concepts connect naturally inside the flow of building one real service — the way you'd actually encounter them managing a team on the job.

lessons.title: Implementing Link Management
lessons.objective: Understand Open Graph metadata and what an API is — well enough to direct and verify link add / delete / edit, including an Open Graph API that auto-collects each link's title, description, and thumbnail.

blocks.text: With folder management done, we now have Claude implement Ohana Link's core features: adding, deleting, and editing links. The most important new concept this time is the Open Graph API, which automatically fetches extra information about any external link — understand it, and you can tell whether the "auto-fill" Claude delivers actually works.

steps.title: Open Graph: where the extra info comes from

blocks.text: Making users type in a title, description, and thumbnail every time they save a link would be painful. That's why most services fill this in automatically from just the URL. Here's how:

Inside a web page's HTML are Open Graph tags that summarize the page's title, description, and thumbnail. Think of them like the shipping label on a package — metadata that gathers the page's key facts in one place.
If we fetch the HTML of the link the user typed and extract just the Open Graph tags, we get all the extra info we need.

steps.title: Why the browser can't make that request itself

blocks.text: Browsers restrict many cross-origin reads unless the other website allows them through CORS. A server-side API can fetch public page metadata and return the specific information your app needs.

The reason is security. That request could carry along personal information the user has stored in the browser — saved passwords, card numbers, and the like. So browsers stop pages from firing off direct requests to outside servers in the first place.
The solution is to route around it through our Next.js server:
The browser asks our Next.js server: “get me the Open Graph info for this link.”
The Next.js server contacts the external link on the browser's behalf and receives the HTML.
The server extracts just the Open Graph tags and responds to the browser.
Think of it like a kid who can't ask their strict dad for a toy directly — so they ask mom, and mom talks to dad. Our Next.js server plays the role of mom.

This pattern — a server that receives a request, performs a defined action, and sends back a response — is what programmers call an API. Return Open Graph info and it's an Open Graph API; return weather data and it's a weather API; return government statistics and it's a public-data API. In the next step, Claude builds our own Open Graph API — and you verify it works.
